                              SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                 PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR          §                        BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY           §
LLC AND LCRA TSC TO AMEND           §                                       OF
THEIR CERTIFICATES OF               §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY           §                        ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST            §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL                  §
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE §
IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,   §
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,             §
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, §
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,    §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES             §

    SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13

                                      I.      INTRODUCTION

       The Commission remanded two issues to this tribunal for supplemental briefing. See

SOAH Order No. 35, Item No. 6597. Issue 11 asks whether the proposed facilities are necessary

to meet state or federal reliability standards. Issue 13 asks what congestion cost savings they will

produce for consumers. Applicants and PUC Staff answer neither question about this line. They

answer Issue 11 with a regional plan, a deference rule, and orders from other dockets. They dismiss

Issue 13 as unnecessary and then offer figures comparing one statewide plan with another.

       The answer to Issue 11 is no. No study isolates this line, ERCOT says only two of the three

765-kV paths are needed by 2030, and the load the plan was built to serve is unsubstantiated. The

answer to Issue 13 is that the record contains no estimate at all, and the plan-level numbers show

the 765-kV plan costing consumers about $136 million more than the 345-kV plan in 2034. The

record is closed, so these gaps cannot be filled.




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                1
                                 II.     GOVERNING STANDARDS

       Applicants must prove that the certificate “is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public.” Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a). In deciding, the Commission

considers, among other factors, “the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional service,”

the effect on the applicant and on other utilities serving the area, community and environmental

values, and “the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers.” See Goeke v.

Hous. Lighting & Power Co., 797 S.W.2d 12, 14 (Tex. 1990) (quoting former PURA § 54(b)–(c)).

ERCOT’s recommendation earns great weight only when its forecasted load is “substantiated by

quantifiable evidence of projected load growth.” 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii),

(ii)(II). Agency expertise “cannot be a substitute for proof,” R.R. Comm’n of Tex. v. Lone Star Gas

Co., 611 S.W.2d 908, 911 (Tex. Civ. App.—Austin 1981, writ ref’d n.r.e.), and every finding needs

“some reasonable basis in the record,” R.R. Comm’n of Tex. v. Torch Operating Co., 912 S.W.2d

790, 792 (Tex. 1995). A project that is not a reliability project must pass the economic test, which

compares its estimated cost to consumers with its estimated congestion savings. Tex. Util. Code §

37.056(d); see 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i); Comm’n Staff’s Initial Br. on Remand

at 3 (Oct. 7, 2026) (“Staff Br.”) (quoting Chairman Thomas Gleeson Mem. at 2 (Sept. 9, 2026)).

         III.    ISSUE 11: APPLICANTS HAVE NOT SHOWN THAT THIS LINE IS
                     NECESSARY TO MEET ANY RELIABILITY STANDARD.

   A. A plan that resolves system-wide violations does not prove that each of its components
      is necessary, and no study isolates this line.

       Applicants never prove that this line is necessary to cure the violations ERCOT found in

its 2030 and 2038 system models. They argue instead that “a project required to cure NERC

reliability violations is, by definition, needed to provide reliable service,” and that Import Path 2

is “unquestionably” a reliability project because it is “part of the identified solution.” Applicants’




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                  2
 Br. on Prelim. Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 at 4, 6 (Oct. 7, 2026) (“Applicants’ Br.”); accord Staff

Br. at 2-3.

        The record contains no such proof. Applicants’ need witness knows of no study that isolated

this line; ERCOT studied the three paths together. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:17-45:4 (Gurley); Applicants’

Br. at 11. ERCOT ran the studies, and no ERCOT witness testified. Tr. Vol. 4 at 49:4-9 (Gurley).

Applicants did not analyze the necessity of the facilities themselves, Tr. Vol. 3 at 228:8-11

(Gurley), and their witnesses could not explain ERCOT’s models beyond the reports, Tr. Vol. 4 at

49:15-50:10 (Gurley and Martin).

        The ALJs correctly found that “the record neither establishes independent need for Import

Path 2 nor that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030.” Proposal for Decision § VII.D.6 (Item No. 6441)

(“PFD”); see id. proposed FOFs 128-31. Nothing on remand disturbs that finding.

        ERCOT’s reduced-load sensitivity confirms the gap. With roughly 20 GW less load, “major

portions” of each plan “will still be needed,” but “significantly fewer 345-kV upgrades (new and

existing) will be needed under both plans.” Applicants’ Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at v-vi.

ERCOT never says Import Path 2 is among the surviving major portions.

    B. “Great weight” depends on substantiated load, and this load was not substantiated.

        Rule 25.101 extends great weight only to a review built on forecasted load “substantiated

by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth.” 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii).

Applicants ignore that condition when they claim that each of four ERCOT documents “is entitled

independently to ‘great weight’” that the ALJs are required to give. Applicants’ Br. at 9. The load

here is unsubstantiated at every level:

        The oil-and-gas load rests on a 2022 S&P Global study that Applicants did not verify. Tr.

Vol. 2 at 45:19-47:6 (Gurley). The forecast nearly doubles in a single year, from 12,240 MW in




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                               3
 2029 to 23,659 MW in 2030. Id. at 45:19-46:16.

       About 59% of the 11,695 MW of non-oil-and-gas load is cryptocurrency mining. Id. at

144:1-10 (Gurley). That load has historically curtailed during constraints. Tr. Vol. 4 at 45:12-16

(Martin). The forecast also included officer-letter load with no signed interconnection agreement.

Tr. Vol. 2 at 148:1-149:1 (Martin). Applying ERCOT’s own 2025 realization-rate methodology

reduces the non-oil-and-gas load by at least 3,571 MW. PFD proposed FOF 92. Staff’s witness

agreed that the forecast was built under the methodology that Senate Bill 6 directed the

Commission to replace, and that reevaluation may be warranted. Tr. Vol. 3 at 286:17-287:21

(Poole).

       Nor are the later documents independent. Applicants concede that the 2024 and 2025 RTPs

“assume the Import Path 2 Projects are in service,” Applicants’ Br. at 11, and the 2025 RTP placed

the full 765-kV STEP in its “starting base cases,” id. at 9, 13, 30. A model that assumes the line

exists cannot confirm that it is needed.

   C. The Far West Import GTCs are operating limits that ERCOT is managing, not a
      “violation” of FAC-011-4, and they point to local generation.

       No FAC-011-4 violation appears in the record. Applicants call the Far West Texas Import

GTCs “a second and independent NERC violation” and say that “failure to build Import Path 2

eliminates the solution to ERCOT’s identified FAC-011-4 violation.” Applicants’ Br. at 7-8. But

their own witness describes FAC-011-4 as the standard under which a system operating limit

“becomes an IROL.” Applicants’ Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 11. Designating an IROL is compliance,

not breach; ERCOT is “monitoring” and managing these constraints. Applicants’ Ex. 14, Ex.

CMM-R-3 at 3.

       The GTC evidence does not isolate this line either. ERCOT’s exit strategy contains six

projects for the North-Far West GTC and eight for the South-Far West GTC. Applicants’ Ex. 14



SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                              4
 (Martin Reb.) at 16-17. Mr. Martin did not author that study or run its analyses. Tr. Vol. 4 at 39:21-

40:8 (Martin). He conceded that the Far West concern arises on low-wind nights and “stems from

a localized generation deficit.” Tr. Vol. 3 at 213:12-214:8, 217:4-14 (Martin); see Applicants’ Ex.

14 (Martin Reb.) at 10.

       The remedy for a local generation deficit is local generation, and it is coming. The exit

strategy assumes only about 2,500 MW of new dispatchable Permian generation. Applicants’ Br.

at 8. The ALJs found 37 planned or announced Permian gas projects totaling about 39.467 GW,

PFD proposed FOFs 142-43, and 71 GW of gas generation in the queue, 20 GW of it targeted for

West Texas, PFD § VII.D.8. They also found that “the Far West Import GTCs do not cure the

evidentiary deficiencies in the forecasted loads.” Id. § VII.D.4.

   D. ERCOT itself said that only two of the three 765-kV paths are needed by 2030, so this
      line is not needed today.

       ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter states that only two of the three 765-kV

import paths are needed by 2030, which defeats Applicants’ claim that the line is “needed today.”

Applicants’ Br. at 18. Their witness conceded it: “The words on the page say that two of the three

are needed.” Tr. Vol. 4 at 10:10-11 (Martin).

       Import Path 2 originated as part of the 2038 solution. Tr. Vol. 2 at 43:2-14 (Gurley). ERCOT

evaluated the 765-kV option “for the 2038 Permian Basin region load level.” Applicants’ Ex. 1

(Application), Att. 5 (PBRP) at 42-44. Staff itself wrote that “all the 765 kV import paths were

given a 2038 reliability need date by ERCOT.” A figure labeling a “765-kV Core Plan needed in

2030,” Applicants’ Br. at 9, does not override ERCOT’s written sequencing. See PFD proposed

FOF 131.




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                  5
    E. Applicants cannot shift their burden to the intervenors by faulting them, for not
      running the study Applicants never ran.

         Intervenors need not disprove necessity; Applicants must prove it. Tex. Util. Code §

37.056(a). Applicants invert that burden by arguing that “the record contains no power-flow study

or other technical analysis modeling a reliable alternative with those facilities removed.”

Applicants’ Br. at 11. Their fallback, that removing Import Path 2 “would introduce an untested

variable,” id. at 11-12, is an admission: the line is untested because Applicants chose not to test it.

They concede that “the applicants did not independently evaluate alternatives.” Id. at 14.

         Staff adds a signature, not evidence. Its witness did no independent need study, alternatives

analysis, or cost review. Tr. Vol. 3 at 274:1-18 (Poole). Its Issue 11 discussion rests on Applicants’

Exceptions and Directory of Evidence, plus three lines of Mr. Poole’s direct testimony. Staff Br. at

2-3 & nn.1-7.

   F. The Commission’s orders on other lines, built on other records, cannot supply
      findings for this line.

         Findings here must rest on this record, not on orders about other lines. Torch Operating,

912 S.W.2d at 792. Applicants ask the ALJs to copy findings from the Commission’s orders on

Import Path 1 (Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315) and Import Path 3 (Docket No. 59336), arguing

that “[t]here is no valid reason to reach a different conclusion for Import Path 2.” Applicants’ Br.

at 11. The Import Path 3 order issued on September 18, 2026, after the PFD and after this record

closed. Id. at 10. Applicants’ own witness agreed that the PBRP orders did not automatically grant

a certificate and that each proceeding must establish every PURA requirement. Tr. Vol. 2 at 42:10-

19 (Gurley). The ALJs reserved need for decision in this docket. SOAH Order No. 24, Docket No.

59182.




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                   6
         This record contains line-specific evidence that defeats the copied findings. The ALJs

found that “the record does not establish that Bell County East can supply power allegedly needed

to flow west into the Permian Basin.” PFD § VII.D.5; see id. proposed FOFs 122-27. Applicants

never determined whether Central Texas generation can serve local data-center load and export

west at design capacity, and ran no sensitivity analysis. Id. proposed FOFs 123-26. Staff’s witness

agreed that the real need is in West Texas and that the project will not lower costs for Bell County

consumers. Tr. Vol. 3 at 253:19-254:2 (Poole). Applicants’ new emphasis on eastbound export

relief, Applicants’ Br. at 8-9, describes a congestion benefit for Issue 13, not a reliability standard.

See Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.) at 13-14.

    G. Proposed Findings of Fact on Issue 11

        SWG Briggs I, L.P. requests the following findings:

    1. No study isolates the need for this line apart from the three 765-kV paths, and Applicants

        did not independently analyze its necessity or alternatives. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:17-45:4

        (Gurley); Tr. Vol. 3 at 228:8-11 (Gurley); Applicants’ Br. at 11.

    2. ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter states that only two of the three 765-kV

        paths are needed by 2030. Tr. Vol. 4 at 10:10-11 (Martin).

    3. ERCOT’s forecasted load was not substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load

        growth.

    4. The record does not establish that this line is necessary to resolve the Far West Texas Import

        GTCs or that local dispatchable generation could not resolve them.

    5. The record does not establish that Bell County East can supply the power this line would

        carry west.




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                    7
       IV.     ISSUE 13: THE RECORD CONTAINS NO ESTIMATE OF CONGESTION
              COST SAVINGS FROM THIS LINE, AND THE PLAN-LEVEL NUMBERS
                         THAT DO EXIST CUT AGAINST APPLICANTS.

    A. The Commission asked for an estimate of this project’s savings, and neither
       Applicants nor Staff supplies one.

        The record contains no estimate of the congestion savings that “may result from the

proposed transmission facilities,” which is the question Issue 13 asks. Applicants answer that “a

congestion cost savings analysis is not required,” Applicants’ Br. at 23, and Staff calls it “not

necessary,” Staff Br. at 3.

        The Commission remanded Issue 13 because the PFD did not answer it. See Chairman

Thomas Gleeson Mem. (Sept. 9, 2026); SOAH Order No. 35. Because this line is not a reliability

project, the economic showing is mandatory and § 37.056(d) requires a comparison of the cost “of

the transmission project” with the savings “that may result from the transmission project.” Tex.

Util. Code § 37.056(d).

        No witness isolated this line’s costs or benefits. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley).

Applicants’ reliability witness offered no opinion on the cost of Import Path 2 and compared it to

no alternative. Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10-13 (Martin). Staff did no independent cost analysis. Tr. Vol. 3 at

275:4-7 (Poole). No test of this line appears under ERCOT’s System-Wide Gross Load Cost

methodology, which compares levelized savings with the first three years’ average annual revenue

requirement. ERCOT, Congestion Cost Savings Test Evaluation Guideline, Version 1.0, § 2 (Jan.

30, 2025). The closed record cannot now supply one. SOAH Order No. 35.

    B. Every savings figure Applicants cite compares one statewide plan with another, not
       this line with the existing system.

        Each savings figure Applicants cite measures the entire statewide 765-kV STEP against a

hypothetical 345-kV plan: “approximately $229 million in additional annual consumer energy cost




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                  8
 savings,” “$28 million in additional annual production cost savings,” “$890 million less in

construction-related outage costs,” and “560 GWh per year in reduced energy losses.” Applicants’

Br. at 18-19. No one estimates what these facilities will save compared with the existing system.

       Applicants cannot settle even on the plan-level number: “over $270 million in annual cost

savings” and “1,443 miles of upgrades” on page 17, but “$229 million” on page 18. Applicants’

Br. at 17-18. Their exhibit reports “approximately $229 million more savings in consumer energy

cost each year” and “approximately 1400 miles fewer existing upgrades.” Applicants’ Ex. 3

(Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 22.

       Historical, system-wide congestion is no substitute. The Independent Market Monitor’s

$10 billion figure for 2020 through 2024, Applicants’ Br. at 17, says nothing about what this line

would relieve.

   C. The savings projections rest on the same unsubstantiated load forecast.

       Overstated load means overstated savings. ERCOT’s 2025 RTP economic cases “used the

2024 RTP final reliability cases as the start cases, specifically the 2027 summer peak case and the

2030 summer peak case with the 765-kV STEP incorporated.” Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.),

Ex. JG-R-3 at 46. The ALJs found the non-oil-and-gas load overstated by at least 3,571 MW. PFD

proposed FOFs 132-35. ERCOT has since warned that many large loads “may not materialize on

time, at full scale, or at all.” ERCOT, Preliminary Long-Term Load Forecast for 2026-2032, Project

No. 58777, Item No. 38.

       Applicants never compared this line’s cost with local generation, Tr. Vol. 4 at 42:23-43:2

(Martin), though Staff’s witness agreed that Path 2-area gas generation could “potentially” cost

ratepayers less, Tr. Vol. 3 at 262:11-21 (Poole), and 71 GW of gas sits in the queue, PFD § VII.D.8.




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13                                9
     D. Proposed Findings of Fact on Issue 13

        SWG Briggs I, L.P. requests the following findings:

    6. The record contains no estimate of congestion savings attributable to this line, and no

        witness isolated its costs or benefits. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley); Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10-

        13 (Martin); Tr. Vol. 3 at 275:4-7 (Poole).

    7. The record’s savings figures compare the statewide 765-kV STEP with a 345-kV plan, not

        this line with the existing system. Applicants’ Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at v-vi.

    8. In 2034, the 765-kV plan costs consumers about $136 million more than the 345-kV plan

        and saves about $63 million against the base case. Id.

    9. The economic projections rely on the unsubstantiated load forecast. Applicants’ Ex. 17

        (Gurley Reb.), Ex. JG-R-3 at 46.

                                 V.     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

        On Issue 11, SWG Briggs asks the ALJs to find that Applicants have not shown that the

Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV line is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards,

to adopt proposed findings 1 through 5, and to decline Applicants’ request to import findings from

the Commission’s orders in Docket Nos. 59029, 59315, and 59336.

        On Issue 13, SWG Briggs asks the ALJs to find that the record contains no estimate of

congestion cost savings attributable to these facilities and that Applicants have not made the

comparison that Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(d) requires, and to adopt proposed findings 6 through 9.

        SWG Briggs I, L.P. further asks the ALJs to issue a supplemental proposal for decision

recommending that the Commission deny the Application, and to grant SWG Briggs I, L.P. all

other relief to which it is entitled.

projects for the North-Far West GTC and eight for the South-Far West GTC. Applicants' Ex. 14

       IV.      ISSUE 13: THE RECORD CONTAINS NO ESTIMATE OF CONGESTION
               COST SAVINGS FROM THIS LINE, AND THE PLAN-LEVEL NUMBERS

    A. The Commission asked for an estimate of this project's savings, and neither
       Applicants nor Staff supplies one.

        The record contains no estimate of the congestion savings that "may result from the

proposed transmission facilities," which is the question Issue 13 asks. Applicants answer that "a

congestion cost savings analysis is not required," Applicants' Br. at 23, and Staff calls it "not

necessary, " Staff Br. at 3.

        The Commission remanded Issue 13 because the PFD did not answer it. See Chairman

Thomas Gleeson Mem. (Sept. 9,2026); SOAH Order No. 35. Because this line is not a reliability

project, the economic showing is mandatory and § 37.056(d) requires a comparison of the cost "of

the transmission proj ect" with the savings "that may result from the transmission proj ect." Tex.

Util. Code § 37.056(d).

        No witness isolated this line's costs or benefits. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley).

Applicants' reliability witness offered no opinion on the cost of Import Path 2 and compared it to

no alternative. Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10-13 (Martin). Staff did no independent cost analysis. Tr. Vol. 3 at

275:4-7 (Poole). No test of this line appears under ERCOT's System-Wide Gross Load Cost

methodology, which compares levelized savings with the first three years' average annual revenue

requirement. ERCOT, Congestion Cost Savings Test Evaluation Guideline, Version 1.0, § 2 (Jan.

30,2025). The closed record cannot now supply one. SOAH Order No. 35.

    B. Every savings figure Applicants cite compares one statewide plan with another, not
        this line with the existing system.

        Each savings figure Applicants cite measures the entire statewide 765-kV STEP against a

hypothetical 345-kV plan: "approximately $229 million in additional annual consumer energy cost
